title: ASIC warns scammers are using AI to spin vast webs of deception

reading.body:
This incident is an impersonation fraud in which AI-generated content, including deepfake images and video, was used to fabricate a news article featuring real, named public figures. The article falsely depicted a confrontation between a senior government official and a known financial journalist in order to promote an unlicensed cryptocurrency platform. The failure is not a model behaving unexpectedly within a legitimate deployment, it is a deliberate misuse of generative AI tools to produce convincing disinformation at scale.

The place in the pipeline where this could have been caught is publication and distribution. Fabricated content of this kind reaches victims because platforms hosting or circulating it apply no check against the identities of the real people depicted or the licensing status of the financial products promoted. ASIC's figures show the volume of such content is large enough that manual review alone would not be sufficient, yet automated detection was not preventing distribution at the scale the regulator describes.

What is not established is who specifically produced the fake article, how the deepfake tools were obtained, or whether any platform knowingly hosted the content. ASIC's report documents the scale and trend, but the regulator's warning is not a finding of liability against any named party.

reports.title: The fake Alan Kohler interview that shows a type of scam that’s on the rise
AI deepfake scams 'an emergency in the making' as ASIC reports rise in false investment endorsements
ASIC warns scammers are using AI to spin vast webs of deception

summary:
A fake online article featuring Reserve Bank governor Michele Bullock and ABC finance presenter Alan Kohler has surfaced as part of a growing wave of AI-generated investment scams. The fabricated article claimed Bullock stormed out of an interview with Kohler over questions about Boulder Sparhaven, an unlicensed cryptocurrency trading platform. The Australian Securities and Investments Commission reports that such scams are becoming increasingly common and sophisticated, using deepfake images and videos of celebrities and politicians to appear legitimate.

ASIC's new research reveals dramatic increases in fraud activity, with the regulator taking down 19,400 scams last year, representing a 182 percent increase. Phishing scams jumped 279 percent, while fake investment platforms rose 151 percent. Prime Minister Anthony Albanese is the most commonly impersonated figure, followed by other politicians and business leaders like Alan Kohler. ASIC advises consumers to verify Australian Financial Services licence numbers through official registers before investing and warns that polished content and familiar branding do not guarantee legitimacy.
